question: to the Commission Sabine Verheyen (PPE), Ralf Seekatz (PPE) Subject:

A recent investigation by Investigate Europe1 has found that Soft2bet, a company based in Cyprus and Malta, operates nearly 150 illegal online casinos that are blacklisted by regulators across the Member States. The scheme reportedly generated EUR 600 million over four years, with funds allegedly also being processed through EU-regulated electronic money institutions. This investigation further alleges that a payment company associated with the scheme obtained authorisation from Visa and Mastercard to process card payments and that Paysafe may be processing deposits from these platforms. 1.
Is the Commission aware of allegations that card networks may be authorising payment companies linked to operators blacklisted by gambling regulators in Member States?

What steps is the Commission taking to ensure that card networks and payment service providers carry out adequate due diligence against national gambling blacklists before authorising merchants or processing payments?

In the light of these allegations, does the Commission consider that current legislation, such as Regulation (EU) 2024/1624, is sufficient to prevent payment service providers from facilitating unlicensed online gambling?

answer: (English version) to the Commission Sabine Verheyen (PPE), Ralf Seekatz (PPE) (22 July 2026) Subject: Payment authorisations facilitating unlicensed online gambling in the EU A recent investigation by Investigate Europe (1) has found that Soft2bet, a company based in Cyprus and Malta, operates nearly 150 illegal online casinos that are blacklisted by regulators across the Member States. The scheme reportedly generated EUR 600 million over four years, with funds allegedly also being processed through EU-regulated electronic money institutions. This investigation further alleges that a payment company associated with the scheme obtained authorisation from Visa and Mastercard to process card payments and that Paysafe may be processing deposits from these platforms. 1. Is the Commission aware of allegations that card networks may be authorising payment companies linked to operators blacklisted by gambling regulators in Member States? 2. What steps is the Commission taking to ensure that card networks and payment service providers carry out adequate due diligence against national gambling blacklists before authorising merchants or processing payments? 3. In the light of these allegations, does the Commission consider that current legislation, such as Regulation (EU) 2024/1624, is sufficient to prevent payment service providers from facilitating unlicensed online gambling? (8 September 2026) The Commission has taken note of the allegations. However, it does not have any investigatory powers in relation to such individual cases. Any assessment of wrongdoing in specific cases is a matter for competent authorities at national level, including regulators, supervisors and law enforcement authorities. Payment service providers, e-money institutions, as well as providers of gambling services established in the EU are subject to the EU anti-money laundering framework, which requires obliged entities to apply risk-based customer due diligence (CDD), including in relation to the nature of the business and the risk profile of the customer and to conduct ongoing monitoring of the business relationship. The rules include an obligation to cease a business relationship where full compliance with CDD requirements is not possible. Under Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 of the European Parliament and of the Council on the prevention of the use of the financial system for the purposes of money laundering or terrorist financing (1), which will apply from 10 July 2027 and will be directly applicable across all Member States, those obligations are strengthened and harmonised. The Commission considers that regulation (EU) 2024/1624 substantially strengthens the EU's framework to prevent the financial system, including payment service providers and electronic money institutions, from being misused to facilitate illicit activity. The Commission and the EU Anti-Money Laundering Authority will continue to monitor emerging risks in relation to payment services and unlicensed gambling.
